paras: The threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain occurred at Monticello, White County, Indiana, on May 26, 1888, when crowds gathered at the jail holding Chamberlain, who had been indicted for the murder of Ida Wittenberg and recaptured after a jailbreak in which Sheriff Henderson was badly beaten. State militia guarded the jail, an armed party approaching the town halted or broke up, and officers later moved Chamberlain secretly to the Michigan City penitentiary. Papers across the country reported a lynching as expected, and Chamberlain later hanged himself in jail at Logansport during his trial in December.

According to the Indianapolis Journal, Chamberlain was accused of shooting Ida Wittenberg, the daughter of a Reynolds family, at the door of her home after she returned from church with another suitor; she died ten days later. To keep him from a mob he was held at Delphi and then Lafayette, and in early May he was returned to Monticello and indicted for first-degree murder. His trial was then postponed to the September term.

On the evening of May 24, Chamberlain and two prisoners held for highway robbery, Benson and Catterson, attacked Sheriff Henderson with iron bars, fracturing his skull and breaking his arm, and fled. Hundreds of men searched the country, the county commissioners offered $800 for Chamberlain, and Benson was retaken the next day. A Delphi dispatch said it was "the general opinion" that Chamberlain would never return to Monticello alive, while the Journal's correspondent thought a lynching improbable, though it "would have been probably different" on the night of the escape.

Chamberlain was captured on the evening of May 25 asleep at the house of his uncle, William Biddle, after his cousins alerted neighbors, who bound him and brought him to Monticello early on May 26. A Delphi wire instead placed the capture near Delphi.

By morning the town was full, and the Indiana State Sentinel's correspondent wrote that despite individual calls for lynching no danger seemed to threaten until a militia company from Delphi under Captain Edward Gresham arrived on the afternoon train. Judge Gould had telegraphed Governor Gray for the troops, and Adjutant General Koontz followed. Both the Sentinel and a Chicago Times special said the soldiers' arrival enraged the crowd, and the Sentinel reported repeated threats of lynching as some 1,500 people gathered. It added that if the sheriff died, his friends and those of the murdered woman were expected to "make short work of Chamberlain."

That night, a Wabash dispatch to the New-York Tribune said, a "band of four hundred armed lynchers" from Reynolds halted on the outskirts, deterred by the militia's rifles. The Sentinel's correspondent, checking a report of 100 men a mile west of town, found about fifty who lacked organization and disbanded. Later, according to Deputy Sheriff J. Richie, he, Koontz, Gresham and John Day took Chamberlain out through an alley and by wagon to Delphi and train to Peru, from where he was sent on May 29 to the Michigan City penitentiary for safekeeping. Richie believed a lynching attempt would most likely have been made otherwise.

Benson was sentenced by Judge Gould on May 26 to five years in prison. In September Chamberlain was brought to Logansport on a change of venue; the Journal reported he had refused food for nineteen days and seemed relieved to be away from White County. On December 3, during the trial, he was found hanged in his cell by a strip of bed-ticking, and jurors told the Journal they would almost unanimously have fixed the death penalty. No report of arrests among the crowd at Monticello appears in the coverage.

The white press treated Chamberlain's guilt as settled before trial, calling him "the murderer," "the desperado" and "the Dual Murderer." Headlines centered on the threat: "A Mob Deterred by the Militia" in the New-York Tribune, "A Lynching Imminent" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, and "In Danger of Lynching" in the Savannah Morning News, reprinting the New York Sun. The Tribune spoke of "Judge Lynch's court" and remarked that the girl's "crime was in discarding the worthless fellow."

Indiana papers carried the fullest reports, and the Sentinel's special recorded local censure of Judge Gould for calling troops from Delphi, "the scene of the Amer Green lynching." Short wire versions of the escape and capture ran in Tennessee, Minnesota, Arkansas, Georgia and Ohio between May 27 and June 2. When Chamberlain died, the Indianapolis Journal headed its report "Gone to a Higher Court" and wrote that the community "breathes easier."

The Tribune put the armed party from Reynolds at 400, while the Sentinel's correspondent, who said he went to the group, counted about fifty. Names also varied: the murdered woman appears as Ella Wittenberg in some dispatches and the sheriff as James rather than Joseph Henderson in the Tribune. The militia was the Delphi company under Gresham in the Sentinel, "Company H" in the Sun account, and "Company A" in the Chicago Times special.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain
bases: Crowds gathered at the Monticello jail with repeated threats to lynch Chamberlain and an armed party approached the town, but militia guarded the jail and he was removed, so the episode is a threatened lynching (A7, A11, A12).

Groups of armed men gathered to lynch Chamberlain for the murder of Ida Wittenberg and the assault on the sheriff, but no one was killed; Chamberlain was taken away under guard and later died by his own hand in the Logansport jail (A7, A11, A12, A18).

Independent specials from Monticello (Indiana State Sentinel, Chicago Times), Wabash (New-York Tribune) and Delphi agree that a crowd threatened a lynching and militia guarded the jail (A6, A7, A9, A11).

accounts.gist: Lynching talk grew after an unrequested militia company arrived; 1,500 people came in and threats were frequent, but a reported band of 100 proved to be about fifty unorganized men who disbanded.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune Wabash dispatch
accounts.gist: Men from three counties came to see Chamberlain lynched; 400 armed lynchers from Reynolds halted on the outskirts, deterred by the militia.

accounts.label: Chicago Times / New York Sun specials
accounts.gist: Cousins turned Chamberlain in to neighbors who bound him; troops sent to prevent a lynching only increased the excitement.

accounts.label: Deputy Sheriff Richie
accounts.gist: Officers slipped Chamberlain out through an alley and away to Peru and Michigan City, believing a lynching attempt would otherwise have been made.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'A Mob Deterred by the Militia', spoke of 'Judge Lynch's court' and wrote that the girl's 'crime was in discarding the worthless fellow'.
The Sentinel's local special reported the threats and resentment at the troops without comment and noted censure of Judge Gould.
Wire versions headed 'A Lynching Imminent', 'In Danger of Lynching' and 'Chamberlain Captured' ran in Minnesota, Tennessee, Arkansas, Georgia and Ohio.
